title: Ἑρμῆς ἀπαντᾷ
about: Priam washes his hands, takes the cup from his wife and prays in the courtyard to Zeus: let him reach Achilles dear and pitiable, and let a bird be sent on the right. Zeus sends an eagle whose wings spread as wide as a rich man’s door, and the Trojans rejoice. Priam drives out of the palace, the herald Idaeus ahead with the mules and wagon, Priam behind with the horses, and his kin follow him lamenting. When they reach the plain and the kin turn back, Zeus sees the two and tells Hermes to bring Priam to Achilles unseen. Hermes ties on his golden sandals, takes his wand and comes to Troy in the likeness of a young prince. At the tomb of Ilus, where Priam has stopped to water the animals at dusk, Idaeus sees the stranger and warns Priam, who stands frozen with fear. Hermes takes Priam’s hand and asks why he is out in the night with treasure, offers help, and Priam sees a good omen in the meeting. Hermes asks whether he is sending his goods away or fleeing the city; Priam asks who he is. Hermes answers that he is a Myrmidon, one of seven sons and a follower of Achilles, who has seen Hector in battle, and that the Achaeans will fight around the town at dawn.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα καὶ ἀμφίπολον ταμίην ὄτρυν’ ὃ γεραιὸς
χερσὶν ὕδωρ ἐπιχεῦαι ἀκήρατον·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and the old man urged on the attendant housekeeper
to pour pure water over his hands;
sentences.i: So he said, and the old man urged the attendant housekeeper to pour pure water over his hands;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί is the stock opening ‘he spoke, and …’, here leading straight into an action. ὃ γεραιός is ‘the old man’, Priam, the article doing the work of a pronoun. ἀμφίπολον ταμίην are two nouns side by side, ‘an attendant, a housekeeper’, the object of ὄτρυν’ (ὄτρυνε, ‘urged on’). ἐπιχεῦαι is the epic aorist infinitive of ἐπιχέω ‘pour over’, and χερσίν is ‘over his hands’. ἀκήρατον ‘pure’ means unmixed and untainted; its derivation is not certain.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ παρέστη
χέρνιβον ἀμφίπολος πρόχοόν θ’ ἅμα χερσὶν ἔχουσα.
sentences.l:
and she stood beside him,
the attendant, holding a washing-basin and a pitcher together in her hands.
sentences.i: and the attendant stood beside him, holding a washing-basin and a pitcher in her hands.
sentences.n: ἣ δὲ παρέστη is ‘and she stood beside him’, the housekeeper of the last line, now called ἀμφίπολος ‘attendant’. χέρνιβον is a vessel for washing the hands, taken here as a basin (the word may also mean the water for it); πρόχοον is a ‘pitcher’, the jug the water is poured from. ἅμα χερσὶν ἔχουσα is ‘holding together in her hands’.

sentences.t: νιψάμενος δὲ κύπελλον ἐδέξατο ἧς ἀλόχοιο·
sentences.l: And having washed, he received the cup from his own wife;
sentences.i: When he had washed his hands, he took the cup from his wife;
sentences.n: νιψάμενος is the aorist middle participle of νίζω, ‘having washed’ (his own hands, as the last lines prepared). κύπελλον is a ‘cup’. ἐδέξατο is ‘received’. ἧς ἀλόχοιο is ‘from his own wife’: ἧς is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative ‘which’, and the genitive names the giver. She is Hecuba, who brought the wine in the last part; the Greek does not name her here.

sentences.t:
εὔχετ’ ἔπειτα στὰς μέσῳ ἕρκεϊ, λεῖβε δὲ οἶνον
οὐρανὸν εἰσανιδών, καὶ φωνήσας ἔπος ηὔδα·
sentences.l:
He prayed then, standing in the middle of the enclosure, and poured the wine
looking up at heaven, and lifting his voice spoke a word:
sentences.i: Then he stood in the middle of the enclosure and prayed, and poured the wine as he looked up at heaven, and lifting his voice he spoke:
sentences.n: The first line, and οὐρανὸν εἰσανιδών after it, are the words of 16.231, and the English of that unit is kept for them. εὔχετ’ is ‘prayed’; στάς is the aorist participle ‘standing, having taken his stand’; μέσῳ ἕρκεϊ is ‘in the middle of the enclosure’, a courtyard, and the Greek does not say whose. λεῖβε is ‘poured’ (a libation) and εἰσανιδών ‘looking up at’. φωνήσας is ‘lifting his voice’ and ἔπος ηὔδα ‘spoke a word’, with ηὔδα the imperfect of αὐδάω.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ Ἴδηθεν μεδέων κύδιστε μέγιστε
δός μ’ ἐς Ἀχιλλῆος φίλον ἐλθεῖν ἠδ’ ἐλεεινόν,
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, from Ida ruling, most glorious, greatest,
grant me to come to Achilles dear and pitiable,
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, you who rule from Ida, most glorious, greatest, grant that I come to Achilles as one dear to him and worthy of his pity,
sentences.n: The opening quotation mark begins Priam’s prayer. The first line is the invocation of 3.276, and its English is kept. Ἴδηθεν is ‘from Ida’, the mountain above Troy, μεδέων ‘ruling’, and κύδιστε and μέγιστε are vocatives, ‘most glorious, greatest’. δός is the aorist imperative of δίδωμι ‘grant’, with μ’ (με) the subject of ἐλθεῖν ‘to come’. φίλον and ἐλεεινόν agree with με: ‘dear’ (φίλος can also mean ‘friendly’, and the Greek does not say which) and ‘pitiable’, one to be pitied. ἐς Ἀχιλλῆος is ‘to Achilles’, the genitive after ἐς with ‘house’ understood.

sentences.t:
πέμψον δ’ οἰωνὸν ταχὺν ἄγγελον, ὅς τε σοὶ αὐτῷ
φίλτατος οἰωνῶν, καί εὑ κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον,
sentences.l:
and send a bird of omen, a swift messenger, which to yourself
is dearest of birds, and its strength is greatest,
sentences.i: and send a swift bird of omen as a messenger, the one that is dearest to you of all birds and whose strength is greatest,
sentences.n: πέμψον is the aorist imperative ‘send’. Priam repeats Hecuba’s instruction (24.292) nearly word for word, with ‘ask for’ changed to ‘send’ and ‘to him himself’ to σοὶ αὐτῷ ‘to yourself’, since he now speaks to Zeus. οἰωνός is a bird seen as an omen, and ἄγγελον ‘messenger’. ὅς agrees with οἰωνόν, ‘which’. φίλτατος οἰωνῶν is ‘dearest of birds’. καί εὑ κράτος … μέγιστον is ‘and of it the strength is greatest’, with εὑ a form of ‘of it’.

sentences.t:
δεξιόν, ὄφρά μιν αὐτὸς ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσι νοήσας
τῷ πίσυνος ἐπὶ νῆας ἴω Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων.
sentences.l:
on the right, so that, seeing it myself with my eyes,
trusting in it I may go to the ships of the swift-colted Danaans.”
sentences.i: a bird on the right, so that I may see it for myself with my own eyes and, trusting in it, go to the ships of the Danaans with their swift colts.”
sentences.n: δεξιόν ‘on the right’ agrees with οἰωνόν; the right was the lucky side for a sign. The closing quotation mark ends Priam’s prayer. ὄφρα with the subjunctive ἴω (from εἶμι) is a purpose clause, ‘so that I may go’, and νοήσας is ‘seeing’. πίσυνος is ‘trusting’, with the dative τῷ ‘in it’. Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων is ‘the swift-colted Danaans’, as in Hecuba’s words just before.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος, τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε μητίετα Ζεὺς
αὐτίκα δ’ αἰετὸν ἧκε τελειότατον πετεηνῶν
μόρφνον θηρητῆρ’ ὃν καὶ περκνὸν καλέουσιν.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, praying, and him heard counsellor Zeus,
and at once an eagle he sent, the most perfect of winged things,
the morphnos, the hunter, which they also call the perknos.
sentences.i: So he prayed, and Zeus the counsellor heard him, and at once sent an eagle, the most perfect of winged creatures, the morphnos, the hunter, which they also call the perknos.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος, τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε … is the ordinary line for a prayer that is heard: ‘so he spoke, praying, and him heard …’. μητίετα Ζεύς is ‘Zeus the counsellor’. ἧκε is ‘sent’ (aorist of ἵημι). τελειότατον πετεηνῶν is ‘the most perfect of winged things’: τέλειος is ‘perfect, complete’, and the usual explanation is that the eagle’s sign is the surest to be fulfilled. μόρφνον and περκνόν are two names for a kind of eagle; περκνός is also an adjective ‘dark, dusky’, and the meaning of μόρφνος is not known. θηρητῆρα is ‘hunter’.

sentences.t:
ὅσση δ’ ὑψορόφοιο θύρη θαλάμοιο τέτυκται
ἀνέρος ἀφνειοῖο ἐῢ κληῗσ’ ἀραρυῖα,
τόσσ’ ἄρα τοῦ ἑκάτερθεν ἔσαν πτερά·
sentences.i: As wide as the door of a rich man’s high-roofed chamber, well fitted with its bolts, so wide on either side of him were the wings;
sentences.n: A comparison of size: ὅσση … τόσσ’ is ‘as great as … so great’, and τέτυκται (perfect passive of τεύχω) ‘is made, stands built’. ὑψορόφοιο is ‘high-roofed’, θαλάμοιο ‘chamber’, and ἀνέρος ἀφνειοῖο ‘of a rich man’. ἐῢ κληῗσ’ ἀραρυῖα is ‘well fitted with bolts’: κληῗσι is the dative plural of κληΐς, here a door’s bolt. τοῦ is ‘of him’, the eagle, and ἑκάτερθεν ‘on either side’. The wings spread as wide as a door, so the bird is very large.

sentences.t:
εἴσατο δέ σφι
δεξιὸς ἀΐξας διὰ ἄστεος·
sentences.l:
and it appeared to them
on the right, darting through the town;
sentences.i: and it showed itself to them on the right as it darted through the town;
sentences.n: εἴσατο is the aorist of εἴδομαι ‘appear, show oneself’ (a different verb from εἶδον ‘saw’), and σφι is ‘to them’, the Trojans. δεξιός ‘on the right’ is the lucky side. ἀΐξας is the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart, rush’, and διὰ ἄστεος is ‘through the town’ (ἄστυ is ‘town’).

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ ἰδόντες
γήθησαν, καὶ πᾶσιν ἐνὶ φρεσὶ θυμὸς ἰάνθη.
sentences.l:
and they, having seen it,
rejoiced, and for all in their minds the heart was warmed.
sentences.i: and when they saw it they rejoiced, and the heart was cheered in all their minds.
sentences.n: οἳ δέ is ‘and they’, the Trojans, and ἰδόντες ‘having seen’ the eagle. γήθησαν is the aorist ‘rejoiced’. καὶ πᾶσιν ἐνὶ φρεσὶ θυμὸς ἰάνθη is ‘and the heart was warmed in the minds of all’: ἰάνθη is the aorist passive of ἰαίνω ‘warm, cheer’. The Odyssey has this line, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
σπερχόμενος δ’ ὃ γεραιὸς ἑοῦ ἐπεβήσετο δίφρου,
ἐκ δ’ ἔλασε προθύροιο καὶ αἰθούσης ἐριδούπου.
sentences.l:
And hurrying, the old man mounted his own chariot,
and drove out of the forecourt and the loud-echoing portico.
sentences.i: In haste the old man mounted his chariot and drove out of the forecourt and the loud-echoing portico.
sentences.n: σπερχόμενος is ‘hurrying’, from σπέρχομαι, and ὃ γεραιός ‘the old man’ is Priam again. ἑοῦ … δίφρου is ‘his own chariot’, the genitive after ἐπεβήσετο ‘mounted’ (ἐπιβαίνω). ἐκ δ’ ἔλασε is ‘and drove out’, with ἐκ split from the verb and no object stated. προθύροιο is the ‘forecourt’ and αἰθούσης ἐριδούπου ‘the loud-echoing portico’, as in the Odyssey.

sentences.t:
πρόσθε μὲν ἡμίονοι ἕλκον τετράκυκλον ἀπήνην,
τὰς Ἰδαῖος ἔλαυνε δαΐφρων·
sentences.l:
In front the mules were drawing the four-wheeled wagon,
these Idaeus drove, the wise-minded;
sentences.i: In front mules drew the four-wheeled wagon, and wise-hearted Idaeus drove them;
sentences.n: πρόσθε μέν sets the order of the little column: mules in front (αὐτὰρ ὄπισθεν, ‘but behind’, begins the next unit), horses behind. τετράκυκλον is ‘four-wheeled’ and ἀπήνην ‘wagon’, the mule-wagon that carries the ransom. τάς is feminine plural, ‘these’, the mules, the object of ἔλαυνε ‘was driving’. Ἰδαῖος is Idaeus the herald. δαΐφρων is rendered ‘wise-minded’ in the first layer and ‘wise-hearted’ in the second, the usual explanation; ‘fierce-minded’ is also given, so the sense is disputed.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὄπισθεν
ἵπποι, τοὺς ὃ γέρων ἐφέπων μάστιγι κέλευε
καρπαλίμως κατὰ ἄστυ·
sentences.i: but behind came the horses, which the old man pressed on with his whip as he followed, swiftly through the town;
sentences.n: ἵπποι are the horses of Priam’s own chariot. τοὺς ὃ γέρων is ‘which the old man’, ὃ being the article as a pronoun. ἐφέπων is ‘going after, driving’, and μάστιγι κέλευε is ‘kept bidding with the whip’: κελεύω is ‘bid, order’, here said of animals, so the English of the second layer says ‘pressed on’. καρπαλίμως is ‘swiftly’ and κατὰ ἄστυ ‘through the town’.

sentences.t:
φίλοι δ’ ἅμα πάντες ἕποντο
πόλλ’ ὀλοφυρόμενοι ὡς εἰ θάνατον δὲ κιόντα.
sentences.l:
and his dear ones, all together, followed,
lamenting much, as if he were going to death.
sentences.i: and all his dear ones followed together, lamenting greatly, as if he were going to his death.
sentences.n: φίλοι is ‘dear ones’, kin and friends, without saying which. ἅμα πάντες is ‘all together’ and ἕποντο ‘followed’ (imperfect of ἕπομαι). πόλλ’ ὀλοφυρόμενοι is ‘lamenting much’, with πολλά used as an adverb. ὡς εἰ is ‘as if’, and θάνατον δέ is ‘to death’, the ending -δε marking the direction. κιόντα is the accusative participle of κίω ‘going’, agreeing with an unnamed ‘him’, Priam.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν πόλιος κατέβαν, πεδίον δ’ ἀφίκοντο,
οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ ἄψορροι προτὶ Ἴλιον ἀπονέοντο
παῖδες καὶ γαμβροί, τὼ δ’ οὐ λάθον εὐρύοπα Ζῆν
ἐς πεδίον προφανέντε·
sentences.l:
And when then they had come down from the city and reached the plain,
they for their part turned back again toward Ilium,
the sons and sons-in-law; but the two did not escape far-thundering Zeus,
having come into view on the plain;
sentences.i: When they had come down from the city and reached the plain, the rest, sons and sons-in-law, turned back toward Ilium; but the two of them, as they came into view on the plain, did not escape the notice of Zeus who thunders from afar;
sentences.n: κατέβαν is κατέβησαν ‘went down’, and πεδίον δ’ is πεδίονδε ‘to the plain’, with -δε marking the direction. The first οἳ is the whole company, Priam and Idaeus with the escort, and οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ picks it up, ‘they for their part’, against τὼ δ’ ‘but the two’ (Priam and Idaeus), a dual. ἄψορροι is ‘back again’ and ἀπονέοντο ‘went back’ (ἀπονέομαι). γαμβροί are ‘sons-in-law’; the word can also mean other relatives by marriage. οὐ λάθον is ‘did not escape the notice of’ (aorist of λανθάνω, with the dual subject τὼ), and εὐρύοπα Ζῆν is the accusative ‘far-thundering Zeus’, with the old doubt about εὐρύοπα. προφανέντε is the dual aorist participle ‘having come into view’.

sentences.t:
ἰδὼν δ’ ἐλέησε γέροντα,
αἶψα δ’ ἄρ’ Ἑρμείαν υἱὸν φίλον ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l:
and seeing him, he pitied the old man,
and at once to Hermes, his dear son, face to face he spoke:
sentences.i: and when he saw him he pitied the old man, and at once spoke to Hermes, his dear son, face to face:
sentences.n: ἰδών is ‘having seen’ and ἐλέησε ‘pitied’, the aorist of ἐλεέω. Ἑρμείαν υἱὸν φίλον are accusatives side by side, ‘Hermes, his dear son’; φίλον is the possessive ‘his own dear’, since Hermes is a son of Zeus. ἀντίον ηὔδα is ‘spoke face to face’, the usual way to open a direct speech.

sentences.t:
Ἑρμεία, σοὶ γάρ τε μάλιστά γε φίλτατόν ἐστιν
ἀνδρὶ ἑταιρίσσαι, καί τ’ ἔκλυες ᾧ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα,
sentences.l:
“Hermes, for to you most of all it is dearest
to be a companion to a man, and you listen to whomever you wish,
sentences.i: “Hermes, for it is dearest to you above all to be a companion to a man, and you listen to whomever you wish,
sentences.n: The opening quotation mark begins Zeus’s speech. Ἑρμεία is the vocative. σοὶ … φίλτατον ἐστιν is ‘it is dearest to you’, with the infinitive ἑταιρίσσαι ‘to be a companion to’, a rare verb made from ἑταῖρος ‘companion’, and ἀνδρί ‘to a man’. καί τ’ ἔκλυες is a general statement in the aorist, ‘and you (are one who) listen’; ᾧ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα is ‘to whomever you wish’, a subjunctive in -σθα, the old second-person ending.

sentences.t:
βάσκ’ ἴθι καὶ Πρίαμον κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν
ὣς ἄγαγ’, ὡς μήτ’ ἄρ τις ἴδῃ μήτ’ ἄρ τε νοήσῃ
τῶν ἄλλων Δαναῶν, πρὶν Πηλεΐωνα δ’ ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.l:
Go, set out, and Priam to the hollow ships of the Achaeans
so lead, that neither anyone sees him nor notices,
of the other Danaans, before he arrives at the son of Peleus.”
sentences.i: Be off with you, and lead Priam to the hollow ships of the Achaeans in such a way that none of the other Danaans sees or notices him before he reaches the son of Peleus.”
sentences.n: The closing quotation mark ends Zeus’s speech. βάσκ’ ἴθι is two imperatives, ‘go, set out’, the pair used when a god sends a messenger. ἄγαγ’ is the aorist imperative of ἄγω ‘lead’. The first ὣς is ‘in such a way’ and the second ὡς introduces the aim, ‘so that’; ἴδῃ and νοήσῃ are aorist subjunctives, ‘sees’ and ‘notices’, and τῶν ἄλλων Δαναῶν ‘of the other Danaans’ says who must not. πρίν with the infinitive ἱκέσθαι is ‘before he arrives’. Πηλεΐωνα is ‘the son of Peleus’, Achilles; the δ’ after it is read as δέ, a particle the English does not need.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and did not disobey the guide, Argeïphontes.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the guide, the slayer of Argus, did not disobey.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε is the ordinary line for an order obeyed: ‘so he spoke, and did not disobey’. διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης is ‘the guide, the slayer of Argus’, Hermes; διάκτορος is ‘guide’ in the usual explanation, and ἀργεϊφόντης is an old epithet of disputed meaning, read as ‘slayer of Argus’. The Odyssey has this line, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἔπειθ’ ὑπὸ ποσσὶν ἐδήσατο καλὰ πέδιλα
ἀμβρόσια χρύσεια, τά μιν φέρον ἠμὲν ἐφ’ ὑγρὴν
ἠδ’ ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν ἅμα πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο·
sentences.i: Then at once he bound beneath his feet his fair sandals, immortal and golden, which bore him over the water and over the boundless earth alike, keeping pace with the breath of the wind;
sentences.n: ἐδήσατο is ‘bound on’ (middle of δέω), and πέδιλα ‘sandals’. ἀμβρόσια χρύσεια is ‘immortal, golden’; the English of the Odyssey’s same lines is kept, though ἀμβρόσιος is ‘ambrosial’ elsewhere. τά μιν φέρον is ‘which used to bear him’ (a habitual imperfect). ἠμὲν ἐφ’ ὑγρὴν ἠδ’ ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν is ‘both over the water and over the boundless earth’, with ὑγρήν ‘the wet’, the sea. ἅμα πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο is ‘together with the breaths of the wind’. The Odyssey has these lines of Hermes, and of Athena.

sentences.t:
εἵλετο δὲ ῥάβδον, τῇ τ’ ἀνδρῶν ὄμματα θέλγει
ὧν ἐθέλει, τοὺς δ’ αὖτε καὶ ὑπνώοντας ἐγείρει·
sentences.l:
And he took up his wand, with which the eyes of men he charms,
of whomever he wishes, and others again, even sleeping, he wakes;
sentences.i: And he took up his wand, with which he charms the eyes of whatever men he wishes, and wakes others again even out of sleep;
sentences.n: ῥάβδον is ‘wand’. τῇ τ’ is ‘with which’, and ὄμματα θέλγει ‘charms the eyes’. ὧν ἐθέλει is ‘of whomever he wishes’, a relative clause whose antecedent is ἀνδρῶν in the line before. τοὺς δ’ … ὑπνώοντας ἐγείρει is ‘others again, even sleeping, he wakes’. The Odyssey has these lines, and their English is kept.

sentences.t: τὴν μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχων πέτετο κρατὺς ἀργεϊφόντης.
sentences.l: This in his hands holding, flew the strong Argeïphontes.
sentences.i: Holding this in his hands, the strong slayer of Argus flew on his way.
sentences.n: τὴν is ‘this’, the wand, and μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχων is ‘holding in his hands’, with μετά used with the dative χερσίν. πέτετο is ‘flew’ and κρατύς ‘strong’. ἀργεϊφόντης is ‘the slayer of Argus’, with its meaning disputed. The Odyssey has this line, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
αἶψα δ’ ἄρα Τροίην τε καὶ Ἑλλήσποντον ἵκανε,
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι κούρῳ αἰσυμνητῆρι ἐοικὼς
πρῶτον ὑπηνήτῃ, τοῦ περ χαριεστάτη ἥβη.
sentences.l:
And at once then to Troy and the Hellespont he came,
and he set out to go, resembling a young prince
first-bearded, whose youth is the most graceful.
sentences.i: At once he came to Troy and the Hellespont, and set out on his way in the likeness of a young prince with his first beard, at the age when youth is most graceful.
sentences.n: αἶψα δ’ ἄρα is ‘and at once then’. Τροίην τε καὶ Ἑλλήσποντον ἵκανε is ‘came to Troy and the Hellespont’, the plain by the strait where the ships lie. βῆ δ’ ἰέναι is ‘he set out to go’, ἰέναι being the infinitive of εἶμι. κούρῳ αἰσυμνητῆρι ἐοικώς is ‘resembling a young prince’: κοῦρος is ‘youth’, αἰσυμνητήρ a rare word for a ruler whose sense here is taken from context, and ἐοικώς the perfect participle ‘resembling’. πρῶτον ὑπηνήτῃ is ‘first-bearded’, and τοῦ περ χαριεστάτη ἥβη ‘whose youth is the most graceful’. The last line is said in the Odyssey of Hermes in the same disguise, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν μέγα σῆμα παρὲξ Ἴλοιο ἔλασσαν,
στῆσαν ἄρ’ ἡμιόνους τε καὶ ἵππους ὄφρα πίοιεν
ἐν ποταμῷ·
sentences.i: When they had driven past the great tomb of Ilus, they halted the mules and horses so that they could drink at the river;
sentences.n: μέγα σῆμα is ‘the great tomb’ (σῆμα is a mark over a grave), and Ἴλοιο is ‘of Ilus’, an ancestor of the Trojan royal house. παρέξ is ‘past’, and ἔλασσαν ‘drove’ (aorist of ἐλαύνω). στῆσαν is the transitive aorist of ἵστημι, ‘made stand, halted’. ὄφρα πίοιεν is ‘so that they might drink’, with the optative. ἐν ποταμῷ is ‘in the river’, at its edge.

sentences.t: δὴ γὰρ καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἤλυθε γαῖαν.
sentences.l: for already indeed darkness had come upon the earth.
sentences.i: for darkness had already come on over the earth.
sentences.n: δὴ γάρ is ‘for already’, giving the reason for the halt, and καί adds emphasis. ἐπὶ … ἤλυθε is the split form of ἐπῆλθε, ‘came on over’, with κνέφας ‘darkness, dusk’ as its subject and γαῖαν ‘earth’ as what it comes over.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἐξ ἀγχιμόλοιο ἰδὼν ἐφράσσατο κῆρυξ
Ἑρμείαν, ποτὶ δὲ Πρίαμον φάτο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.l:
And him from close by seeing, noticed the herald,
Hermes; and to Priam he said, and lifted his voice:
sentences.i: The herald saw him from close by and noticed Hermes, and said to Priam, lifting his voice:
sentences.n: κῆρυξ is ‘the herald’, Idaeus. τὸν … Ἑρμείαν are ‘him, Hermes’: the poet names the god, though the herald sees only a young man. ἐξ ἀγχιμόλοιο is ‘from close by’, and ἐφράσσατο ‘noticed’ (aorist of φράζομαι). ποτὶ δὲ Πρίαμον is ‘and to Priam’, with ποτί for πρός. φάτο φώνησέν τε is ‘he said and raised his voice’, an introduction to a speech.

sentences.t: φράζεο Δαρδανίδη· φραδέος νόου ἔργα τέτυκται.
sentences.l: “Take heed, Dardanus’ descendant; of a shrewd mind the works are at hand.
sentences.i: “Take care, descendant of Dardanus: this is work for a shrewd mind.
sentences.n: The opening quotation mark begins the herald’s speech. φράζεο is the imperative of φράζομαι ‘take heed, consider’, and Δαρδανίδη ‘descendant of Dardanus’ is Priam. φραδέος νόου ἔργα τέτυκται is brief, literally ‘of a shrewd mind works have been made’; the usual sense is that the moment calls for a clear head, and the English takes that sense.

sentences.t: ἄνδρ’ ὁρόω, τάχα δ’ ἄμμε διαρραίσεσθαι ὀΐω.
sentences.l: A man I see, and soon I think that we shall be torn apart.
sentences.i: I see a man, and I think that we shall soon be torn to pieces.
sentences.n: ἄνδρ’ ὁρόω is ‘I see a man’, with ὁρόω the open form of ὁράω. τάχα is ‘soon’, and ἄμμε is the Aeolic form of ἡμᾶς ‘us’. διαρραίσεσθαι is the future middle infinitive of διαρραίω ‘tear to pieces, shatter’, passive in sense, and ὀΐω is ‘I think’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ φεύγωμεν ἐφ’ ἵππων, ἤ μιν ἔπειτα
γούνων ἁψάμενοι λιτανεύσομεν αἴ κ’ ἐλεήσῃ.
sentences.l:
But come now, let us flee on the horses, or else him
by the knees taking hold we shall beseech, in case he pities.”
sentences.i: But come, let us flee with the horses, or else take hold of his knees and beg him, in case he takes pity.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή is ‘but come now’. φεύγωμεν is the subjunctive ‘let us flee’, and ἐφ’ ἵππων ‘on the horses’, that is, by driving off. ἤ is ‘or’, and μιν ‘him’. γούνων ἁψάμενοι is ‘having taken hold of his knees’, the suppliant’s gesture. λιτανεύσομεν is ‘we shall beseech’; the form may also be a subjunctive, ‘let us beseech’. αἴ κ’ ἐλεήσῃ is ‘in case he pities’. The closing quotation mark ends the herald’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, σὺν δὲ γέροντι νόος χύτο, δείδιε δ’ αἰνῶς,
ὀρθαὶ δὲ τρίχες ἔσταν ἐνὶ γναμπτοῖσι μέλεσσι,
στῆ δὲ ταφών·
sentences.i: So the herald spoke, and the old man’s wits were thrown into confusion, and he was terribly afraid; the hairs stood upright on his supple limbs, and he stood in amazement;
sentences.n: σὺν … χύτο is a split compound of συγχέω ‘pour together, confuse’, so ‘his mind was confounded’, with γέροντι ‘for the old man’ a dative of the person affected; νόος is a form of νοῦς ‘mind’. δείδιε is a perfect with present sense, ‘is afraid’, and αἰνῶς ‘terribly’. ὀρθαὶ … τρίχες ἔσταν is ‘the hairs stood upright’, with ἔσταν = ἔστησαν used as an intransitive aorist ‘stood’. γναμπτοῖσι μέλεσσι is ‘pliant limbs’. στῆ δὲ ταφών is ‘and he stood in amazement’, with ταφών the aorist participle of the verb behind τέθηπα ‘be amazed’ and τάφος ‘amazement’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἐριούνιος ἐγγύθεν ἐλθὼν
χεῖρα γέροντος ἑλὼν ἐξείρετο καὶ προσέειπε·
sentences.l:
and the helper himself, from close by coming,
the old man’s hand taking, questioned him and addressed him:
sentences.i: but the helper himself came up from close by and, taking the old man’s hand, questioned him and spoke to him:
sentences.n: αὐτός ‘himself’ is Hermes, who now acts in person. ἐριούνιος is ‘the helper’: the meaning of the word is not known, and ‘helper’ is one ancient guess (‘luck-bringer’ is another). ἐγγύθεν ἐλθών is ‘having come from close by’, and χεῖρα γέροντος ἑλών ‘having taken the old man’s hand’. ἐξείρετο is ‘questioned’ (ἐξείρομαι) and προσέειπε ‘addressed’.

sentences.t:
πῇ πάτερ ὧδ’ ἵππους τε καὶ ἡμιόνους ἰθύνεις
νύκτα δι’ ἀμβροσίην, ὅτε θ’ εὕδουσι βροτοὶ ἄλλοι;
sentences.l:
“Where, father, thus the horses and the mules do you steer
through the ambrosial night, when other mortals are asleep?
sentences.i: “Father, where are you steering your horses and mules like this through the ambrosial night, when other mortals are asleep?
sentences.n: The opening quotation mark begins Hermes’ speech. πῇ is ‘where to’, πάτερ ‘father’, a respectful address to an old man, and ὧδε ‘thus, like this’. ἰθύνεις is ‘you steer, you guide straight’. νύκτα δι’ ἀμβροσίην is ‘through the ambrosial night’, the divine night. ὅτε θ’ εὕδουσι is ‘when they sleep’, a general statement, and βροτοὶ ἄλλοι ‘other mortals’.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ σύ γ’ ἔδεισας μένεα πνείοντας Ἀχαιούς,
οἵ τοι δυσμενέες καὶ ἀνάρσιοι ἐγγὺς ἔασι;
sentences.l:
And did not even you fear the Achaeans, breathing might,
who to you are ill-disposed and hostile, close at hand?
sentences.i: Are not even you afraid of the Achaeans, who breathe might and are ill-disposed and hostile to you, close by?
sentences.n: οὐδὲ σύ γ’ ἔδεισας is ‘did not even you fear’, with ἔδεισας the aorist of δείδω. μένεα πνείοντας is ‘breathing might’: μένεα is the plural of μένος ‘might, fighting spirit’, and Ἀχαιούς is the noun the participle goes with. οἵ τοι is ‘who to you’, τοι being σοι. δυσμενέες ‘ill-disposed’ and ἀνάρσιοι ‘hostile’ are two different words. ἐγγὺς ἔασι is ‘are close by’, with ἔασι the epic form of εἰσί.

sentences.t:
τῶν εἴ τίς σε ἴδοιτο θοὴν διὰ νύκτα μέλαιναν
τοσσάδ’ ὀνείατ’ ἄγοντα, τίς ἂν δή τοι νόος εἴη;
sentences.l:
If any one of them should see you through the swift black night
bringing so many helpful things, what then would your mind be?
sentences.i: If any of them saw you in the swift black night bringing so many helpful things, what would you then think?
sentences.n: τῶν εἴ τίς σε ἴδοιτο is a condition with the optative, ‘if any one of them should see you’, with τῶν ‘of them’, the Achaeans. θοήν is ‘swift’ and νύκτα μέλαιναν ‘black night’. τοσσάδ’ ὀνείατ’ ἄγοντα is ‘bringing so many helpful things’: ὀνείατα is the plural of ὄνειαρ ‘a help, a benefit’, here the goods on the wagon. τίς ἂν δή τοι νόος εἴη is ‘what, then, would your mind be?’, that is, what would you have in mind.

sentences.t:
οὔτ’ αὐτὸς νέος ἐσσί, γέρων δέ τοι οὗτος ὀπηδεῖ,
ἄνδρ’ ἀπαμύνασθαι, ὅτε τις πρότερος χαλεπήνῃ.
sentences.l:
Neither are you yourself young, and old is this one who keeps you company,
to ward off a man, when anyone first grows angry.
sentences.i: You are not young yourself, and the man who keeps you company is old, too old to ward off a man whenever someone is the first to grow angry.
sentences.n: οὔτ’ … γέρων δέ sets two facts side by side: ‘neither are you young, and this companion is old’. νέος is ‘young’ and γέρων ‘old’. τοι οὗτος ὀπηδεῖ is ‘this one keeps company with you’; ὀπηδέω is ‘attend, keep company with’, here of Idaeus. ἄνδρ’ ἀπαμύνασθαι is ‘to ward off a man’, an infinitive of result after the idea ‘too old’, which the Greek leaves unsaid. The second line is also an Odyssey line, and its English is kept. ὅτε τις πρότερος χαλεπήνῃ is ‘when anyone first grows angry’, a general condition.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ οὐδέν σε ῥέξω κακά, καὶ δέ κεν ἄλλον
σεῦ ἀπαλεξήσαιμι· φίλῳ δέ σε πατρὶ ἐΐσκω.
sentences.l:
But I shall do you no harm, and even another
I would ward off from you; to my dear father I liken you.”
sentences.i: But I shall do you no harm, and I would even keep another away from you; I liken you to my own dear father.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ οὐδέν σε ῥέξω κακά is ‘but I shall do you no harm’: ῥέξω is the future of ῥέζω ‘do’, with κακά ‘evils’ as its object and οὐδέν strengthening the denial. καὶ δέ κεν ἄλλον σεῦ ἀπαλεξήσαιμι is ‘and I would even ward off another from you’, with the optative and κεν ‘would’, and σεῦ the genitive ‘from you’. φίλῳ δέ σε πατρὶ ἐΐσκω is ‘and I liken you to my dear father’; ἐΐσκω is ‘liken’, and φίλῳ is the possessive ‘my own dear’. The closing quotation mark ends Hermes’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα γέρων Πρίαμος θεοειδής·
sentences.l: Him then answered the old man Priam, godlike in form:
sentences.i: Then Priam, the old man, godlike in form, answered him:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα is the regular opening of a reply: ἠμείβετο is ‘answered’, ἔπειτα ‘then’, and τὸν ‘him’, Hermes. γέρων Πρίαμος is ‘the old man Priam’, and θεοειδής is ‘godlike in form’.

sentences.t: οὕτω πῃ τάδε γ’ ἐστὶ φίλον τέκος ὡς ἀγορεύεις.
sentences.l: “Thus in some way these things are, dear child, as you say.
sentences.i: “So it is, dear child, just as you say.
sentences.n: The opening quotation mark begins Priam’s speech. οὕτω πῃ is ‘thus, in some way’, with πῃ the indefinite adverb, a softening word the English does not repeat. τάδε γ’ ἐστί is ‘these things are’, φίλον τέκος ‘dear child’, a kind address to a younger stranger, and ὡς ἀγορεύεις ‘as you say’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔτι τις καὶ ἐμεῖο θεῶν ὑπερέσχεθε χεῖρα,
ὅς μοι τοιόνδ’ ἧκεν ὁδοιπόρον ἀντιβολῆσαι
αἴσιον,
sentences.l:
But still, some one of the gods has held his hand over me too,
who sent such a wayfarer to meet me,
auspicious,
sentences.i: But some one of the gods has held his hand over me as well, in sending me such a traveller to meet, a good omen,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἔτι τις is ‘but still some one’. θεῶν ὑπερέσχεθε χεῖρα is ‘of the gods held his hand over’: to hold a hand over someone is to shield him, and ὑπερέσχεθε is an aorist of ὑπερέχω. ἐμεῖο is ‘me’, with καί ‘too’. ὅς μοι τοιόνδ’ ἧκεν … ἀντιβολῆσαι is ‘who sent such a one to meet me’, with ἧκεν the aorist of ἵημι and ἀντιβολῆσαι the aorist infinitive ‘to meet’. ὁδοιπόρον is ‘wayfarer’, a traveller on the road. αἴσιον is ‘auspicious, of good omen’, from αἶσα ‘fitting share’; Priam takes the meeting as a good sign.

sentences.t:
οἷος δὴ σὺ δέμας καὶ εἶδος ἀγητός,
πέπνυσαί τε νόῳ, μακάρων δ’ ἔξεσσι τοκήων.
sentences.l:
such as you are, in body and form admirable,
and you are prudent in mind, and of blessed parents you are born.”
sentences.i: such a one as you, admirable in build and in looks, and prudent in mind; you are born of blessed parents.”
sentences.n: οἷος δὴ σύ is ‘such a one as you indeed (are)’. δέμας καὶ εἶδος are two accusatives of respect, ‘in body and in form’. ἀγητός is ‘admirable’. πέπνυσαι is the perfect of πινύσκω, ‘you are prudent’, with νόῳ ‘in mind’. μακάρων δ’ ἔξεσσι τοκήων is ‘and you are from blessed parents’, with ἔξεσσι = ἐξ ἐσσί ‘you are of’. The closing quotation mark ends Priam’s speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the guide, Argeïphontes:
sentences.i: Then the guide, the slayer of Argus, said to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is the formula ‘and then, in turn, he addressed him’, with αὖτε marking that the turn to speak passes to the other. διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης is ‘the guide, the slayer of Argus’, Hermes, here named only by his epithets.

sentences.t: ναὶ δὴ ταῦτά γε πάντα γέρον κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπες.
sentences.l: “Yes indeed, all this, old man, according to what is fitting you have said;
sentences.i: “Yes indeed, old man, all this you have said as is fitting;
sentences.n: The opening quotation mark begins Hermes’ speech. ναὶ δή is ‘yes indeed’, and κατὰ μοῖραν ‘according to what is fitting’ (μοῖρα is ‘due measure, one’s share’). ἔειπες is the aorist of εἶπον, ‘you have said’. This line stands word for word at 1.286, and its English is kept.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον,
sentences.l: But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly;
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly:
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, and μοι ‘to me’. τόδε εἰπέ is ‘tell this’. ἀτρεκέως is ‘exactly’ and κατάλεξον the aorist imperative of καταλέγω ‘recount, set out’. The line is a stock request for an exact account and stands at 10.384, and its English is kept. The colon in the second layer leads into the double question that follows.

sentences.t:
ἠέ πῃ ἐκπέμπεις κειμήλια πολλὰ καὶ ἐσθλὰ
ἄνδρας ἐς ἀλλοδαποὺς ἵνα περ τάδε τοι σόα μίμνῃ,
sentences.l:
whether somewhere you are sending out treasures, many and good,
to foreign men, so that these things may remain safe for you,
sentences.i: whether you are sending your many good treasures out somewhere to foreign men, so that these may stay safe for you,
sentences.n: ἠέ … ἦ ἤδη (the next unit) is the pair ‘whether … or’, continuing the request of the line before: ‘tell me whether …’. πῃ is ‘somewhere’, and ἐκπέμπεις ‘you are sending out’. κειμήλια is ‘treasures’, things laid up, with πολλὰ καὶ ἐσθλά ‘many and good’. ἄνδρας ἐς ἀλλοδαπούς is ‘to men of another land’, foreigners. ἵνα περ is ‘so that’, with the subjunctive μίμνῃ ‘may remain’, and σόα ‘safe’, the plural of σόος agreeing with τάδε ‘these things’.

sentences.t:
ἦ ἤδη πάντες καταλείπετε Ἴλιον ἱρὴν
δειδιότες·
sentences.l:
or by now all of you are leaving sacred Ilium,
fearing;
sentences.i: or whether by now you are all leaving sacred Ilium in fear;
sentences.n: ἦ ἤδη is the second half of the ‘whether … or’ pair: ‘or (whether) by now’. πάντες is ‘all (of you)’, and καταλείπετε ‘you are leaving behind’. Ἴλιον ἱρήν is ‘sacred Ilium’. δειδιότες is the perfect participle of δείδω, ‘fearing’, in its reduplicated epic form.

sentences.t:
τοῖος γὰρ ἀνὴρ ὤριστος ὄλωλε
σὸς πάϊς·
sentences.l:
for such a man, the best, has perished,
your son;
sentences.i: for such a man, the best, has perished: your son;
sentences.n: τοῖος … ἀνήρ is ‘such a man’, so great a one; ὤριστος is ὁ ἄριστος by crasis, ‘the best’; ὄλωλε is the perfect of ὄλλυμι, ‘has perished’. σὸς πάϊς is ‘your son’, with πάϊς for παῖς. The ano teleia after πάϊς ends the clause.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι μάχης ἐπιδεύετ’ Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l: for in no way was he lacking in battle with the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: for he was in no way lacking in battle against the Achaeans.”
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι is ‘for in no way’. ἐπιδεύετ’ is the imperfect ἐπιδεύετο, ‘was lacking’ (the elided ending could also be the present ἐπιδεύεται, but Hector is dead, so the past is meant). ἐπιδεύομαι takes the genitive of what is lacked, μάχης ‘in battle’, and Ἀχαιῶν is taken with μάχης, ‘battle with the Achaeans’ (it could also be read with ἐπιδεύετ’ itself, so the Greek leaves the construction open). The closing quotation mark ends Hermes’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα γέρων Πρίαμος θεοειδής·
sentences.l: Him then answered the old man Priam, godlike in form:
sentences.i: Then Priam, the old man, godlike in form, answered him:
sentences.n: The same line as 24.372: ἠμείβετο is ‘answered’, γέρων Πρίαμος ‘the old man Priam’, θεοειδής ‘godlike in form’, and τὸν ‘him’ is Hermes again.

sentences.t: τίς δὲ σύ ἐσσι φέριστε τέων δ’ ἔξεσσι τοκήων;
sentences.l: “And who are you, best of men, and of what parents are you born?
sentences.i: “Who are you, then, best of men, and from what parents do you come?
sentences.n: The opening quotation mark begins Priam’s speech. τίς δὲ σύ ἐσσι is ‘and who are you’, and φέριστε is the vocative ‘best of men’, a polite address. τέων is the Ionic form of τίνων, ‘of which’, and ἔξεσσι τοκήων is ‘you are from parents’ (ἐξ ἐσσί), as in 24.377.

sentences.t: ὥς μοι καλὰ τὸν οἶτον ἀπότμου παιδὸς ἔνισπες.
sentences.l: how finely the fate of my ill-fated son you have told me.”
sentences.i: How well you have told me of the fate of my ill-fated son!”
sentences.n: ὥς is the exclamatory ‘how’, and μοι ‘to me’. καλά is the adverb ‘finely, well’, and ἔνισπες the aorist of ἐνέπω ‘tell’. τὸν οἶτον … παιδός is ‘the fate of the son’, with οἶτον ‘fate’ and ἀπότμου ‘ill-fated, unlucky’. Priam speaks of Hector without naming him. The closing quotation mark ends Priam’s speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the guide, Argeïphontes:
sentences.i: Then the guide, the slayer of Argus, said to him in turn:
sentences.n: The same line as 24.378: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is ‘and then, in turn, he addressed him’, and διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης is ‘the guide, the slayer of Argus’, Hermes.

sentences.t: πειρᾷ ἐμεῖο γεραιὲ καὶ εἴρεαι Ἕκτορα δῖον.
sentences.l: “You make trial of me, old man, and ask about heavenly Hector.
sentences.i: “You are testing me, old man, in asking about heavenly Hector.
sentences.n: The opening quotation mark begins Hermes’ speech. πειρᾷ is the second person of πειράω in the middle, ‘you try, you test’, with ἐμεῖο ‘me’ in the genitive. γεραιέ is the vocative ‘old man’. εἴρεαι is the second person singular of εἴρομαι ‘ask’, with Ἕκτορα δῖον ‘heavenly Hector’ as the person asked about.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ μάλα πολλὰ μάχῃ ἔνι κυδιανείρῃ
ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ὄπωπα, καὶ εὖτ’ ἐπὶ νηυσὶν ἐλάσσας
Ἀργείους κτείνεσκε δαΐζων ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ·
sentences.i: I have seen him many times with my own eyes in the battle that brings men glory, and when he drove the Argives to the ships and kept killing them, cutting them down with sharp bronze;
sentences.n: τὸν μέν ‘him indeed’ is Hector, put first for emphasis, and the object of ὄπωπα, the perfect of ὁράω, ‘I have seen’. μάλα πολλά is ‘very often’. μάχῃ ἔνι κυδιανείρῃ is ‘in the man-glorifying battle’, the battle that brings men glory. καὶ εὖτ’ is ‘and when’ (εὖτε = ὅτε). ἐπὶ νηυσὶν ἐλάσσας is ‘having driven (them) to the ships’, with the participle of ἐλαύνω. κτείνεσκε is a past habitual (the -σκε form), ‘kept killing’, and δαΐζων ‘cutting down’. ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ is ‘with sharp bronze’.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δ’ ἑσταότες θαυμάζομεν· οὐ γὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
εἴα μάρνασθαι κεχολωμένος Ἀτρεΐωνι.
sentences.l:
and we, standing by, marvelled; for Achilles
would not let us fight, being angered at the son of Atreus.
sentences.i: and we stood by and marvelled, for Achilles, angry with the son of Atreus, would not let us fight.
sentences.n: ἑσταότες is the perfect participle ‘standing’, and θαυμάζομεν ‘we marvel’, a present in form telling a past scene, so ‘marvelled’ in English. οὐ γάρ … εἴα is ‘for … was not letting’, the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’, with the infinitive μάρνασθαι ‘to fight’. κεχολωμένος is the perfect participle of χολόομαι ‘angered’, and Ἀτρεΐωνι is the dative ‘at the son of Atreus’, Agamemnon.

sentences.t: τοῦ γὰρ ἐγὼ θεράπων, μία δ’ ἤγαγε νηῦς εὐεργής·
sentences.l: For I am his attendant, and one ship brought me, a well-made one;
sentences.i: For I am his attendant, and one well-made ship brought me;
sentences.n: τοῦ is ‘his’, Achilles’, and θεράπων ‘attendant’. ἐγώ is stressed. μία νηῦς εὐεργής is ‘one well-made ship’, with νηῦς the Ionic nominative of ναῦς. ἤγαγε is ‘brought’, and its object, ‘me’, is left unsaid.

sentences.t: Μυρμιδόνων δ’ ἔξειμι, πατὴρ δέ μοί ἐστι Πολύκτωρ.
sentences.l: Of the Myrmidons I am, and my father is Polyctor.
sentences.i: I am one of the Myrmidons, and my father is Polyctor.
sentences.n: Μυρμιδόνων δ’ ἔξειμι is ‘and I am of the Myrmidons’: ἔξειμι is ἐξ εἰμί ‘I am from’, as ἔξεσσι is ἐξ ἐσσί, and not the future of ἐξέρχομαι. The Myrmidons are Achilles’ people. πατὴρ δέ μοί ἐστι is ‘and my father is’, with the name Πολύκτωρ ‘Polyctor’.

sentences.t:
ἀφνειὸς μὲν ὅ γ’ ἐστί, γέρων δὲ δὴ ὡς σύ περ ὧδε,
ἓξ δέ οἱ υἷες ἔασιν, ἐγὼ δέ οἱ ἕβδομός εἰμι·
sentences.l:
Rich he is, and an old man indeed, just like you here,
and six sons are his, and I am the seventh of them;
sentences.i: He is rich, and he is an old man, just like you; six sons are his, and I am the seventh;
sentences.n: ὅ γ’ is ‘he’, the father, with ἀφνειός ‘rich’. γέρων δὲ δὴ ὡς σύ περ ὧδε is ‘and an old man indeed, just as you are, so’: ὡς σύ περ is ‘just as you’, and ὧδε ‘thus’. ἓξ δέ οἱ υἷες ἔασιν is ‘and six sons are his’, with οἱ ‘to him’ and ἔασιν = εἰσίν. ἕβδομος is ‘seventh’.

sentences.t: τῶν μέτα παλλόμενος κλήρῳ λάχον ἐνθάδ’ ἕπεσθαι.
sentences.l: among them, the lot being shaken, I obtained by lot to follow here.
sentences.i: When lots were shaken among us brothers, I drew the lot to follow here.
sentences.n: τῶν μέτα is ‘among them’, the brothers. παλλόμενος κλήρῳ is ‘with the lot shaken’: παλλόμενος is a participle of πάλλω ‘shake’, and the grammar is loose, but the sense is that lots were cast. λάχον is the aorist of λαγχάνω ‘obtain by lot’, with the infinitive ἕπεσθαι ‘to follow’, and ἐνθάδ’ is ‘here’.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἦλθον πεδίον δ’ ἀπὸ νηῶν·
sentences.l: And now I have come to the plain from the ships;
sentences.i: Now I have come to the plain from the ships;
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ is ‘but now’. ἦλθον is ‘I came, I have come’. πεδίον δ’ is πεδίονδε ‘to the plain’, with -δε marking the direction, and ἀπὸ νηῶν is ‘from the ships’.

sentences.t:
ἠῶθεν γὰρ
θήσονται περὶ ἄστυ μάχην ἑλίκωπες Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l:
for at dawn
about the town will make battle the quick-eyed Achaeans.
sentences.i: for at dawn the quick-eyed Achaeans will wage battle around the town.
sentences.n: ἠῶθεν is ‘at dawn’. θήσονται μάχην is ‘will make battle’, the future middle of τίθημι with μάχη, a phrase for ‘wage battle’. περὶ ἄστυ is ‘around the town’. ἑλίκωπες Ἀχαιοί is ‘the quick-eyed Achaeans’, with ἑλίκωπες the masculine of an epithet whose sense is disputed.

sentences.t:
ἀσχαλόωσι γὰρ οἵδε καθήμενοι, οὐδὲ δύνανται
ἴσχειν ἐσσυμένους πολέμου βασιλῆες Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
For these chafe, sitting, and are not able
to hold back those eager for war, the kings of the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: For these men sit and chafe, and the kings of the Achaeans cannot hold back their men, who are eager for war.”
sentences.n: ἀσχαλόωσι is ‘chafe’ (from ἀσχαλάω), and οἵδε ‘these here’, the Achaeans; καθήμενοι is ‘sitting’. οὐδὲ δύνανται … ἴσχειν is ‘and are not able to hold back’, with βασιλῆες Ἀχαιῶν ‘the kings of the Achaeans’ as subject, put last for emphasis. ἐσσυμένους is the accusative participle of σεύομαι ‘be eager, rush’, with πολέμου ‘for war’, and agrees with an unstated ‘them’, the men. The closing quotation mark ends Hermes’ speech; Priam replies in the next part.
